o: Design a structure supporting add(number), deleteOne(number) (no-op if absent), and hasFrequency(frequency) (does any number occur exactly `frequency` times?). Up to 2·10⁵ operations, so each must be roughly O(1). The trick is maintaining two maps: value → count, and count → how many values have that count, updating both sides on every add/delete.
k: Keep cnt[value] and freqCnt[count]; hasFrequency(f) is just freqCnt[f] > 0.
When a value's count changes from c to c±1, decrement freqCnt[c] and increment freqCnt[c±1].
deleteOne must check existence first to avoid corrupting freqCnt with negative counts.

a.i: Store counts per value and, inversely, how many values hold each count. Every add/delete performs two O(1) map updates that keep the inverse map consistent; queries become a single lookup.
s: deleteOne(x): if cnt[x] > 0, do the symmetric updates.
a.t: O(1) expected per operation — each add/delete touches a constant number of hash-map entries.
a.sp: O(U) where U is the number of distinct values inserted.

w: The dual-map pattern generalizes to any 'aggregate over counts' query. Pitfalls: calling deleteOne on an absent number (guard with cnt > 0), and answering hasFrequency via cnt.values() scans (too slow). A follow-up: support addMany/deleteMany or report the most common frequency, which may need a heap or ordered map over nonzero frequencies.
